scope: Read-only audit of every authored field in legacy Days 1–10; all 160 questions, 60 corrections, 100 wrong/right worked examples, 47 rule blocks, all rule models/tables/definitions, writing tasks, checklists and examination claims were inspected. No website/project source was edited.
limitations: This is an expert editorial review, not independent consensus or psychometric calibration.
All source URLs cited in supporting_references were fetched with HTTP 200, checked by HTML title and relevant body text. Unlisted claims retain explicit verification limitations.
Some disputed usage requires further specialist reference verification before replacement publication; these are not counted as externally verified rules.
No live learner records or private account state were accessed.
Source-access failures are recorded separately in /tmp/grammar-audit-sources/fetches.json; a retry with a browser User-Agent succeeded for the source register used here.
retained_strengths: Individually authored, topic-aligned practice rather than an unrelated shared bank.
Plain explanations, authentic civic/academic examples, worked reasons and original-writing prompts.
Correction tasks offer models and explicitly avoid exact-string automated marking in the existing interface.
Present-perfect/past distinctions, clause boundaries and broad active production are already present.

issues.quote: A word class is a job, not a name; police ... works like an adjective.
issues.explanation: Word class is grammatical category/form, while subject, object and modifier are functions. Police in police report is normally a noun functioning as a premodifier; descriptive meaning alone does not make it an adjective.
issues.proposed_correction: Distinguish category from function; teach noun modifier police and conversion chair as separate analyses.

issues.proposed_correction: Use several distributional and inflectional diagnostics, with explicitly qualified limits.

issues.quote: Since 2018 requires present perfect continuous; nowadays signals simple; neither paragraph ... a single verb from the other tense
issues.explanation: Present perfect simple can describe repeated continuing issuing. Nowadays can describe current temporary trends with progressive. Literary past can be legitimate. Mixed past and present across explanatory prose can be justified.
issues.proposed_correction: Accept meaningful tense/aspect alternatives; require explicit continuing/current context, and ask learners to justify legitimate tense changes.

supporting_references.title: Stative verbs | LearnEnglish
Past simple or present perfect? - Cambridge Grammar

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: a date ... if one is present, the present perfect is automatically wrong
issues.explanation: A date in a since-phrase or embedded clause is compatible with present perfect; present time spans and event time must be distinguished. Already/just/recently do not mechanically require present perfect, especially in AmE.
issues.proposed_correction: Limit the finished-past prohibition to adverbials locating the perfect event in a finished past period; teach AmE and context variation.

supporting_references.title: Past simple or present perfect? - Cambridge Grammar

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: It is + present perfect + since ... It is three years since the policy was launched.
issues.explanation: The stated formula has no present-perfect verb in its example. Since-clauses can themselves use perfect forms depending on continuing states, so they do not invariably take past simple.
issues.proposed_correction: Write It is/has been + duration + since + past/perfect clause and explain the meaning distinction with verified examples.
issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: past perfect exists purely to prevent ambiguity ... no second past event ... do not use
issues.explanation: Past perfect also supports reported speech, counterfactuals, changed plans and an implicitly established past reference time. A second event need not appear in the same sentence.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach anteriority relative to an explicit or contextual past viewpoint and its other functions.

supporting_references.title: Past perfect simple ( I had worked ) - Cambridge Grammar

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: The roads are still wet because it ____ all night. rained/has rained/has been raining
issues.explanation: Simple past and present perfect simple can both explain wet roads as well as the continuous. Present relevance does not uniquely force progressive.
issues.proposed_correction: Give a continuation cue and ask which choice foregrounds ongoing duration; accept valid alternative interpretations.

supporting_references.title: Past simple or present perfect? - Cambridge Grammar

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: How long ____ you ____ for the result? have/been waiting vs did/wait
issues.explanation: Did you wait is a fully grammatical question about a completed wait. Nothing in the prompt says the person is still waiting.
issues.proposed_correction: Add You are still waiting now or use explanation of ongoing vs completed waits.
issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: I had finished the paper two hours ago; The committee had submitted ... last Friday
issues.explanation: Both past-perfect alternatives can be licensed by a discourse-established later past reference. Without such context simple past is the unmarked default, but the other choices are not universally incorrect.
issues.proposed_correction: Ask for a context-free neutral report explicitly, or provide an explicit reference frame that separates the meanings.

supporting_references.title: Past perfect simple ( I had worked ) - Cambridge Grammar

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: The file ____ on the table where the clerk had left it. lay/was laid down
issues.explanation: Both lay and was laid down yield grammatical, coherent sentences, with different focus/agent implications.
issues.proposed_correction: Replace passive was laid down with an invalid form if testing the past of lie; or ask for the intransitive past form explicitly.
issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: already sits between had and the participle
issues.explanation: Most candidates already had submitted is a legitimate alternative with focus on already, even though had already submitted is more usual. The note mistakes normal placement for a categorical constraint.
issues.proposed_correction: Present had already submitted as the neutral default, and accept already had submitted in a suitable emphasis context.
issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: Neither tense works with a finished time expression.
issues.explanation: The statement bans finished-time expressions with past perfect, contradicting the lesson’s own By 2020 ... had been abandoned example and standard past-perfect usage.
issues.proposed_correction: Distinguish present perfect with finished event-time adverbials from past perfect relative to an earlier/later past frame.

supporting_references.title: Past perfect simple ( I had worked ) - Cambridge Grammar
Past simple or present perfect? - Cambridge Grammar

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.location: terms.Sequence of tenses; rules[3].plain/points; examples[2,5,8]; pitfalls
issues.quote: a universal truth stays present ... pulling it into past misrepresents it as no longer true
issues.explanation: Backshift is frequently optional when truth remains current, and backshifted universal truths do not assert that they have ceased to be true. The source contradicts Day 12’s optionality.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach temporal viewpoint, continued validity and reported-speaker stance; present both legitimate forms with context.

supporting_references.title: Reported speech: indirect speech - Cambridge Grammar

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: will is least committed; I finish my degree next year sounds wrong; going to not will for evidence
issues.explanation: Future constructions overlap. Simple present can express a settled personal schedule, and will can make an evidence-based prediction. Formal writing does not universally prefer passive voice; shall also has formal first-person future uses.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach tendencies and discourse choices with contrasts, not exclusive substitutions.

supporting_references.title: Future: will and shall - Grammar - Cambridge Dictionary
Future: be going to ( I am going to work ) - Cambridge Grammar

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: Never use will in a time or condition clause; connectors already announce future
issues.explanation: When/if can introduce embedded questions, and willingness, result-as-condition and other modal meanings license will/would. The lesson itself gives one exception while the headline/checklist deny any.
issues.proposed_correction: Distinguish future adjunct clauses from content interrogatives and explain willingness/result conditions consistently.

supporting_references.title: Conditionals: if - Grammar - Cambridge Dictionary

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: By + a future point ... future perfect is required
issues.explanation: We will finish by Friday is fully grammatical. By marks a deadline, not a compulsory tense. Future perfect foregrounds completion before a future reference time. An explicit future point may also be understood from context.
issues.proposed_correction: Use meaning contrasts and require the requested future-perfect form only when explicitly assessing that transformation.
issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: The conference ____ on 12 April according to the published schedule. will begin/begins/is going to begin
issues.explanation: All three are grammatical descriptions of a scheduled event. Present simple is a useful conventional default, not an exclusive grammatical answer.
issues.proposed_correction: Ask which form is the present simple for a schedule, or supply a transformation instruction.

supporting_references.title: Future: will and shall - Grammar - Cambridge Dictionary
Future: be going to ( I am going to work ) - Cambridge Grammar

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: currency will be/is going to come under pressure; This time next week ... will write/will have written/will be writing
issues.explanation: The evidence context does not make will ungrammatical. A future point can locate the start, completion or progress of an event depending on what the author intends.
issues.proposed_correction: State the targeted meaning explicitly: activity already in progress at that moment, or prediction with a specified contrast.

supporting_references.title: Future: will and shall - Grammar - Cambridge Dictionary
Future: be going to ( I am going to work ) - Cambridge Grammar

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: By June she will have taught/will have been teaching for twenty years
issues.explanation: Both perfect simple and perfect progressive are grammatical with teach and duration. Progressive foregrounds continuity; simple can summarise the total career duration.
issues.proposed_correction: Ask which form foregrounds ongoing activity or use an explicit structure-identification task.
issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: Indus flows through four provinces
issues.explanation: The precise geographical claim is not sourced and may confuse flowing through with forming a boundary. It is unnecessary for teaching continued truth/backshift.
issues.proposed_correction: Use a simple verified scientific/general fact or an invented clearly labelled scenario; do not introduce unverified geographical assertions.
issues.verification_status: non-linguistic factual claim flagged for verification, not asserted false

issues.quote: A modal is always followed by bare infinitive; ought to listed among modals
issues.explanation: The broad headline includes ought to but immediately names it as an exception. Modal and semi-modal categories vary; negatives can intervene, and finite vs non-finite restrictions need structure-based explanation.
issues.proposed_correction: Define central modals and marginal/semi-modal patterns; present ought to as its own pattern and keep formulas consistent.
issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: official notifications almost always use have to ... shall binding obligation stronger ... might more tentative
issues.explanation: Must can express external rules and is standard in formal notices. Shall is not intrinsically stronger than must; legal drafting depends on jurisdiction/style. May and might do not encode fixed probability levels.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach default speaker/circumstance tendencies, epistemic vs deontic meanings, overlap and style-sensitive legal drafting.

supporting_references.title: Future: will and shall - Grammar - Cambridge Dictionary

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: might not = less likely; should have = the right thing was not done; could have = possible but did not happen
issues.explanation: Might not expresses possible non-occurrence, not merely a fixed lower probability. Should have can express an expectation whose outcome is unknown; could have can express uncertain past possibility. Perfect modal constructions may also concern completion before a future point.
issues.proposed_correction: Provide separate epistemic, evaluative and counterfactual readings and explicit negation scope.
issues.verification_status: expert review; specialist modal-source check required before full replacement publication

issues.quote: each type fixes tense of both halves; never will/would in if-clause
issues.explanation: Pedagogical conditional types do not exhaust real conditionals, speech-act conditions, relevance conditions and modal willingness/result conditions. The source itself contains could in an if clause.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach numbered patterns as a useful starting framework with exceptions and pragmatic uses, preserving a formal default for counterfactual past.

supporting_references.title: Conditionals: if - Grammar - Cambridge Dictionary

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: Use were, not was, after if in unreal conditions
issues.explanation: Irrealis were is the formal default, but was is widespread acceptable informal standard usage with I/he/she/it; its presence alone does not prove a grammatical error.
issues.proposed_correction: Specify formal written register when requiring were, and explain indicative past vs irrealis meanings separately.
issues.verification_status: expert review; full register comparison source required before publication

issues.quote: should ... acceptable in speech but weaker in formal written English; be not should be
issues.explanation: Mandative should is a standard British option in formal as well as informal usage. The lesson mislabels a legitimate form as weaker/nonformal and restricts subjunctive use inaccurately.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach subjunctive and mandative should as legitimate alternatives; explain regional distribution and preserve their equivalent directive reading.

supporting_references.title: Verb patterns: verb + that -clause - Cambridge Grammar

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: She insisted that the report was revised ... -> be revised
issues.explanation: Insist can assert a fact or demand an action. Was revised is a grammatical assertion; be revised expresses a demand and may change intended meaning. Suggest likewise has evidential and recommending senses.
issues.proposed_correction: Provide context choosing insist= demand vs assert, and compare both grammatical constructions.

supporting_references.title: INSIST | English meaning - Cambridge Dictionary
Verb patterns: verb + that -clause - Cambridge Grammar

issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: must not -> need not because the sentence means no obligation
issues.explanation: A literal prohibition is grammatically well-formed; e-registration rules could indeed prohibit extra documents. The course invents the intended policy meaning.
issues.proposed_correction: Supply an explicit no-obligation scenario or ask learners to explain the semantic difference instead of correct a grammatical sentence.
issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.quote: every candidate carries (A) ... and reports (C) ... Key A
issues.explanation: If the task requires the bare subjunctive, both carries in A and reports in C need changing. Moreover indicative mandative constructions vary by region/register, so the instruction must specify the requested form.
issues.proposed_correction: Ask for a complete subjunctive transformation or place both verbs in one answer segment with explicit formal structure requirements.
issues.verification_status: confirmed two-segment repair needed under the item’s stated answer rationale

issues.quote: can’t have signed because on leave; speaks as if he made ... has made/makes
issues.explanation: Being on leave does not preclude remote signing; the modal expresses speaker inference, not logically proven fact. As-if content can describe an ongoing current claim or a completed decision, and lack of authority does not fix tense.
issues.proposed_correction: Make evidential certainty and temporal content explicit; ask for intended modality rather than treat alternative meanings as grammar faults.
issues.verification_status: expert review; source support as listed

issues.location: Days 1–10 examTip, why and explanatory prose
issues.quote: single most tested; signature CSS trap; examiners ... never/always
issues.explanation: No authenticated paper references, count methodology or examiner reports support the repeated frequency, preference and psychometric assertions.
issues.proposed_correction: Replace with original-practice descriptions; retain official-exam claims only after source verification.
issues.verification_status: all 10 day fields reviewed; no supporting examination sources present in authored data

issues.quote: 160 objective items: answer positions A26/B91/C42/D1; 43 spot items; zero no-error options
issues.explanation: Extreme B skew makes the intended answer predictable; all error-spotting items assume an error. Few task types and weak contextual constraints reduce construct validity.
issues.proposed_correction: Review and rebalance distractors and positions after verifying keys; include genuine correct/no-error sentences and production/analysis activities.
issues.verification_status: automatically counted from all 160 authored items

issues.quote: Questions have id/kind/prompt/options/answer/why only
issues.explanation: There are no stable grammatical-concept tags, difficulty levels, abilities, prerequisite mappings, alternative-answer metadata or source registers. Every day has 4 warm-ups, 12 drills and 6 corrections, below the new production targets.
issues.proposed_correction: Create versioned concept-linked content and question models; author additional substantive targeted practice; preserve historical ids in the legacy version.
issues.verification_status: all fields and data model inspected

coverage.present: Word classes, basic countability, linking vs lexical verbs, adjective/adverb choice and function words are present.
coverage.missing_or_inadequate: Morphemes, roots/stems, open/closed classes, inflection/derivation, accurate category/function distinction and a progressive clause framework are absent or inadequate.

coverage.present: Noun-head agreement, subject types, objects/complements, inversion, dummy constructions and participial attachment are present.
coverage.missing_or_inadequate: Valency, full constituent analysis, finite/non-finite distinction, passive attachment nuance, and reliable grammatical diagnostics need development.

coverage.present: Basic finite clause types, clause joining, restrictive/supplementary relatives and connector choices are present.
coverage.missing_or_inadequate: Non-finite clauses, phrase hierarchy, content vs fused relative clauses, extraposed relatives, clause functions and contextual punctuation are missing or misdescribed.

coverage.present: Fragments, fused sentences, comma splices and practical boundary repairs are taught and practised.
coverage.missing_or_inadequate: Contextually licensed fragments, utterance vs clause distinction, rhetorical punctuation and non-local diagnosis need qualification.

coverage.present: Head agreement, and/or/nor, quantifiers, relative agreement, inversion and several special nouns are present.
coverage.missing_or_inadequate: Regional collective agreement, proximity vs notional agreement, titles/mathematical cases, nuanced fractions/measurements and disputed relative agreement are underdeveloped.

coverage.present: Capitalisation, stops/questions, introductory/list/nonrestrictive/coordinate commas and apostrophes are present.
coverage.missing_or_inadequate: Style-guide variation, genuine interrogative requests, letter plurals, contraction has, fuller comma functions and robust punctuation gap validation are missing.

coverage.present: Present/past simple and progressive, stative restriction and tense consistency are present.
coverage.missing_or_inadequate: Title promises eight forms but explicit teaching covers four; forms/negatives/interrogatives, past habit used to/would, dynamic stative senses and narrative viewpoint need expansion.

coverage.present: Present perfect, perfect progressive, past perfect, since/for and irregular participles are present.
coverage.missing_or_inadequate: Advanced repeated/resultative/duration contrasts, contextual reference time, negative/interrogative forms, past-perfect progressive and regional variation are insufficiently developed.

coverage.present: Will/going to, arranged/scheduled futures, perfect/progressive future, future clauses and backshift are present.
coverage.missing_or_inadequate: Future constructions overlap, current relevance/backshift optionality, future-in-the-past, modal exceptions and context-based assessment need substantial correction.

coverage.present: Central modal forms, broad modal meanings, perfect modals, zero/first/second/third/mixed conditionals, irrealis were, inversion and mandative subjunctive are present.
coverage.missing_or_inadequate: Ability/permission/deduction paradigms, marginal modals, didn’t need to vs needn’t have, mood distinctions, formal hedging, pragmatic conditions and mandative-should variation need deep treatment.
